title: EconEvals
question: Can the agent learn to price in a market it can't see?
blurb: The agent prices ten products for 100 rounds. It never sees what customers will pay, and their tastes keep shifting. It has its own past prices, sales and profits to learn from, plus notes it writes to itself. Each model plays four different markets.
footnote: Scores on the Economic Intelligence Index's 0-100 scale, rescaled from the benchmark's own results. The questions below explain the scale.

notes.measures: Learning a market from experience, and adjusting when that market changes.
notes.scoring: The paper measures profit in the second half of the game as a share of the best profit possible. We turn that into a 0-100 score. 0 matches a simple pricing rule that ignores the data. 100 means the best possible prices in every round.
notes.original: In the paper's terms, Claude Opus 5.5 earned 87% of the best possible profit and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 52%. The simple rule earns a large share without learning anything, so raw shares make the field look closer than it is. Our score shows how far each model gets beyond that rule. We use the paper's hardest setting and its model settings.
